newsitem.title: INDONESIA: World Bank says Indonesia's economic future bright.
newsitem.headline: World Bank says Indonesia's economic future bright.

text.p: The World Bank's chief representative in Indonesia on Monday predicted the country's growth would continue to be strong over the next year, although little had been done to reduce domestic risk.
Dennis de Tray told reporters he expected economic growth to be about 7.75 percent this year and he saw "an overall healthy picture for the next six to 12 months".
But he said political concerns continued to hang over the economy, pointing to the run-up to last month's general elections which led to a fall in foreign investment.
"The domestic scene here has not done anything to lower country risk, especially over the last couple of months," he said.
"It's actually been difficult to do business here over the last six months. Government officials have been quite busy with the elections."

The government has said foreign investment approvals during January to May declined to $14.4 billion, a drop of 25.5 percent from the year-ago period. But officials have said the fall was mainly due to the elections and would be made up before the end of the year.
De Tray said he saw Indonesia's exports rising about 10-15 percent this year.

He forecast inflation rising slightly from the projected six percent in the fiscal 1997-98 year (April-March) if the government increased administered prices, such as those for power and fuel, and if agricultural production was below the levels of the last two years.
But he said any slight increase in inflation should not be taken as a sign of a reversal of macroeconomic policy, describing it as essentially a price-related effect.

"This remains an economy which few investors can stay away from for any length of time," he added. "It remains an attractive place to locate export production. If it continues to aggressively follow the policies which have got it here today, this country has a very bright future."

De Tray said although many investors were concerned about the country's political scenario, including the issue of finding a successor to long-ruling President Suharto, the government had been successful in separating the management of the economy from domestic political issues.

"We see no reason to suspect this will not continue along those lines in the future," he said. "Investor confidence in Indonesia reflects the fact that most investors believe that after 30 years of appropriate macroeconomic policies, Indonesia is not about to change the way it does its economic business."

The World Bank said last week that other factors were a cause for concern in Indonesia, including high core inflation, a fall in the pace of deregulation and a banking sector that was weak by international standards and over-exposed to the property sector.

It noted that the current account deficit was likely to increase to about $10.1 billion, or four percent of Gross Domestic Product, in the fiscal 1997/98 year (April-March) from $8.823 billion in 1996/97.
De Tray however said the current account deficit was within manageable proportions and although total debt had increased, government debt had fallen.
He said the central Bank Indonesia needed to reinforce regulation of the banking sector although he did not see any systemic problem in the sector.
